choices.text: A standard an application is certified against
choices.why: That is closer to the ASVS; the Top 10 has no requirements to verify.

choices.text: A list of the main kinds of web risk
choices.why: Right. It says where to look, for the average application.

choices.text: The ten worst vulnerabilities published that year
choices.why: Each entry is a category gathering many weaknesses, not one flaw.

choices.text: The rule set a DAST scanner runs
choices.why: Scanners have their own rules; the list is a document for people.

prompt: Server-side request forgery had its own place, A10, in 2021. Where is it in the 2025 list?
hint: What does the server reach that the user could not?

choices.text: Still at A10, under a new name
choices.why: A10 of 2025 is Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, a new category.

choices.text: Inside A05, Injection
choices.why: The address is not read as a command; the server goes where it should not.

choices.text: Inside A01, Broken Access Control
choices.why: Right. It is an access-control failure, made by the server on the user's behalf.

choices.text: Removed from the list for lack of data
choices.why: It was folded into another category, not dropped.

prompt: Match each 2025 category to a case from this course's services.

pairs.right: a name can be guessed at without limit
a successful sign-in leaves no line
a word in Content-Length is answered 500

prompt: How is 2025's A03, Software Supply Chain Failures, wider than 2021's Vulnerable and Outdated Components?
hint: More than a library with a known flaw.

choices.text: It covers only libraries older than two years
choices.why: Age is not the test; tampering and the build are what was added.

choices.text: It adds tampered dependencies and the build
choices.why: Right. The whole chain, not only a version with an advisory.

choices.text: It moves the subject from libraries to licences
choices.why: Licences are a legal question; the category is about security.

choices.text: It applies to compiled languages and not to Python
choices.why: pip packages are as much a supply chain as any other.

prompt: How do the Top 10 and the ASVS divide the work in a test plan?

choices.text: The ASVS ranks the risks, the Top 10 lists the fixes
choices.why: The other way round, and neither is a list of fixes.

choices.text: The Top 10 is for testers, the ASVS for developers
choices.why: Both serve both; the split is between where and what.

choices.text: Either one alone is enough, they overlap fully
choices.why: The Top 10 has no verifiable requirements; the ASVS has no ranking of where to start.

choices.text: The Top 10 says where, the ASVS what to check
choices.why: Right. Categories first, then the verifiable requirements behind them.

prompt: How many levels does ASVS 5.0.0 define?
hint: The box office aims at the middle one.

prompt: Why are the A06 rows of the plan held by a review rather than by a test?

choices.text: A test checks code against a decision; A06 judges the decision
choices.why: Right. Somebody has to read what was decided and say if it holds up.

choices.text: Design flaws are too slow to test on every change
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; there is no assertion to write.

choices.text: A scanner already covers design, so a test adds nothing
choices.why: No scanner of lesson 16 reads a design decision.

choices.text: The rows are not finished and need a test later
choices.why: That is the meaning of to write, a different value of the column.

prompt: In the plan, registration refusing a password under 12 characters is marked to write. What does that say?
hint: Does the code check it today?

choices.text: The check is missing from account.py
choices.why: register refuses it today; what is missing is the test.

choices.text: Nothing would notice if the check went
choices.why: Right. A debt with a name.

choices.text: A scanner checks it on a schedule
choices.why: That would be the scanner value of the column.

choices.text: It is a design decision for a person to review
choices.why: Its result can be asserted: a 400 for a short password.

prompt: A test marked @unittest.expectedFailure holds finding F19-1. What happens on the day somebody fixes the page?
hint: The run counts the opposite of what it expected.

choices.text: The test passes quietly and the run stays OK
choices.why: unittest reports an unexpected success, and the run fails.

choices.text: unittest deletes the marker by itself
choices.why: Nothing edits the file; a person removes it.

choices.text: The run fails with an unexpected success
choices.why: Right. The reminder to remove the marker so the test holds the fix.

choices.text: The test is skipped from then on
choices.why: Skipping is a different decorator, and it would hide the fix.

prompt: A request with Content-Length: many gets {"error": "something went wrong"} and 500. What is the finding?

choices.text: The body leaks the traceback
choices.why: It holds one sentence; the traceback stayed in the server's log.

choices.text: The status should be a 400
choices.why: Right. The client was wrong, and the server says it failed.

choices.text: The server should have logged nothing
choices.why: Logging the full error on the server is the right half of the split.

choices.text: The request should have been let through
choices.why: Refusing it is right; letting it through would be failing open.

prompt: Finding F19-1 is fixed by sending the bookings page with Cache-Control: no-___.
Which of these log lines keeps the rule of this lesson?
hint: Four things in, one thing never.

choices.text: failed sign-in for 'sam' with password 'a guess'
choices.why: It carries the password that was tried.

choices.text: refused GET /staff/bookings to account 1: staff only
choices.why: Right. Who, what, outcome and why, with the time in front, and no secret.

choices.text: request refused
choices.why: Nobody can tell who, or what was asked for.

choices.text: session started for account 1, token Ivd5VrccSr9Ce2M53_is6HMw
choices.why: A token in a log is a session anybody reading it can use.

prompt: account.py writes names into its log with %r. What does that stop?
hint: The probe had a line break in it.

choices.text: A name forging a line of its own
choices.why: Right. The break is written as \n, on the line it belongs to.

choices.text: A password reaching the log
choices.why: The password is kept out by never passing it to the logger at all.

choices.text: SQL in a name reaching the database
choices.why: That is the parameters' job, lesson 20; %r is about the log.

choices.text: A very long name filling up the disk
choices.why: %r does not shorten anything.

prompt: Why is a successful sign-in with no log line rated medium, above the other two findings?
hint: A stolen password does not fail.

choices.text: Successes are far more common than failures
choices.why: Frequency is not the reason; what the line would prove is.

choices.text: It breaks a law on keeping records
choices.why: The lesson rates it by what an investigation loses.

choices.text: It slows down every sign-in
choices.why: A missing line costs no time.

choices.text: It is the one trace of a stolen password
choices.why: Right. And here there is none.

prompt: Put in order the steps from the Top 10 to a row of the test plan.
hint: Choose the level before the requirements.
items: choose the ASVS level the system aims at
find the ASVS requirements behind it
write each one as a test case that can fail

prompt: account.py gains a feature: the avatar is fetched from an address the customer types. Which row of the plan changes, and how?
hint: A server reaching where the user cannot.

choices.text: A05: the address is tested for SQL
choices.why: The risk is where the server goes, not a command in the text.

choices.text: A01: its SSRF row moves from review to a test
choices.why: Right. A test that an address on 127.0.0.1 or an internal network is refused.

choices.text: A03: the fetched image is a dependency
choices.why: A customer's picture is data, not something the software is built from.

choices.text: None: uploads are already checked by content
choices.why: The content check comes after the fetch; the fetch itself is the new risk.

prompt: Which of these rows can an automated test hold? Choose every one.

choices.text: Every answer carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
choices.why: Right. A header compared on three paths.

choices.text: Locking a name after five failures is the right design
choices.why: Whether it is right is a judgement: a review.

choices.text: A failed sign-in is logged without the password
choices.why: Right. assertLogs reads the line.

choices.text: A malformed body is answered 400
choices.why: Right. Four bodies, four statuses.

choices.text: Abuse cases are written for every new feature
choices.why: A habit of the team, checked by a person.

prompt: A teammate says the plan is weak because only nineteen of its thirty-eight rows are tests. What is the better reply?
hint: What do the other values of the column mean?

choices.text: Agreed: every row should be turned into a test
choices.why: Design and deployment rows have no assertion to write.

choices.text: Rows held by a review or a scanner are held as well
choices.why: Right. Each value says honestly how the row is checked.

choices.text: The count is irrelevant once a pentest is booked
choices.why: A pentest looks once a year; the plan runs every day.

choices.text: Tests are weaker than reviews, so fewer is better
choices.why: Each holds what the other cannot; neither replaces the other.
